episodes.212803: A cold front backed south and westward through eastern and central NM during the early morning hours of June 14th. Abundant low-level moisture pushed in behind this front, reaching the Continental Divide. This provided fuel for thunderstorm development during the early afternoon hours of the 14th with on such severe thunderstorm producing severe wind gusts in Rio Rancho. Afternoon thunderstorms developed again over the northern mountains and along the central mountain chain of NM June 15th. There were reports of 8 inch tree branches down in Taos landing over power lines from severe thunderstorm wind gusts. Other thunderstorms advanced eastward off the Sangre de Cristo Mountains organizing into a line producing severe wind gusts through northeastern NM. This line of storms over northeastern NM eventually advanced all the way through east-central NM and into the TX Panhandle. Severe wind gusts reaching 60 mph or more were observed in Guadalupe County, including at Santa Rosa Lake State Park.
episodes.212899: Storms produced strong winds across portions of central, north central and northeast South Dakota during the afternoon of June 15th. A peak wind gust of 69 mph was recorded on the South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) mesonet station 5 miles west of Seneca (Potter county), with a 68 mph gust recorded on the SDDOT mesonet station in Waubay (Day county). Rapidly decaying showers also generated strong winds in Lyman and Buffalo counties, with a 66 mph gust recorded on the SDDOT station 5 miles north of Reliance and a 64 mph gust on the SDDOT station 3 miles north of Gann Valley.
episodes.212945: A significant flash flooding event began across South Texas on June 15, 2026 as an exceptionally moist tropical air mass overspread the region ahead of a slow-moving frontal boundary and an upper-level disturbance lifting out of northern Mexico. Deep tropical moisture associated with the remnants of former Tropical Storm Cristina and a developing low-pressure area near the Texas coast pushed precipitable water values into the 2.3-2.7 inch range, near or above daily record levels and roughly three standard deviations above normal for mid-June. At the same time, abundant instability, saturated atmospheric profiles, and deep warm cloud layers supported highly efficient rainfall production, with rainfall rates frequently reaching 2-4 inches per hour and locally approaching 5 inches per hour. A slow-moving mesoscale convective system that had developed farther north sagged southward into South Texas while repeated bands of thunderstorms trained over the same locations along the frontal boundary and zones of strong low-level moisture convergence. Weak steering currents and persistent inflow from the Gulf allowed storms to repeatedly redevelop over affected areas, producing localized rainfall totals of 3-5 inches in only a few hours and ultimately widespread totals of 4-8 inches. The combination of extreme rainfall rates, repeated training convection, and prolonged moisture transport resulted in dangerous flash flooding across portions of the Coastal Plains, Coastal Bend, Rio Grande Valley, and surrounding areas.
episodes.213272: Over the course of the weekend, a meandering front and an unseasonably strong upper trough triggered widespread showers and thunderstorms across the region. Heavy rain from training storms ultimately resulted in flash flooding, particularly affecting several Central Texas counties. A significant flood event occurred in and around Waco costing millions of dollars.
episodes.213342: Increasing heat and humidity led to scattered strong to severe thunderstorms. One particularly intense cluster resulted in wind gusts estimated to 80 mph in Frederick County, Maryland.
episodes.213354: Increasing heat and humidity led to scattered strong to severe thunderstorms.
episodes.213603: An upper-level low which had been nearly stationary over Hudson Bay in Canada was producing several disturbances moving across the upper Midwest in early to mid-June.  On June 15th, enough mid-level instability and surface moisture was in place to generate scattered showers and thunderstorms that afternoon. In Mille Lacs County, one storm briefly pulsed up strong enough to produce a 67-mph wind gust approximately 9 miles north of Milaca. The storm continued southeast into Isanti County where a couple trees were downed in Dalbo and Stanchfield.
episodes.213894: A low pressure system stations across central Quebec with a trailing cold front across the Great Lakes allowed for central Pennsylvania to experience residence time within the warm sector throughout much of the day on June 14, 2026. Initial shower activity during the morning and early afternoon hours stayed largely non-hazardous before convection began across western Pennsylvania during the afternoon and evening hours. Clearing skies after the initial showers and thunderstorms allowed for instability to rise above 1000 J/kg across much of the region by the late afternoon hours with effective bulk shear in the 40-50 knot range. Of note, 0-1km shear magnitudes across much of the region trended upwards of 30 knots, which allowed for ample low-level spin within thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours. As the cold front began to move eastward across central Pennsylvania, a line of thunderstorms pushed across the region with many kinks in the line exhibiting tornadic circulations. Ahead of the line, some thunderstorms began to form where clear skies allowed for destabilization with some cells exhibiting supercellular characteristics. Wind damage was first observed during the early evening hours, where multiple trees and wires were down across western Pennsylvania. Damage continued as thunderstorms moved further east throughout the evening hours. In terms of cells ahead of the line, wind damage was mostly concentrated across Franklin, York, and Lancaster Counties. Four tornadoes occurred with the storm system on June 14th; an EF-1 near Grand Valley in Warren County, an EF-0 near Homer Township in Potter County, an EF-1 near Pine Glen in Centre County, and an EF-1 near Kirkwood in Lancaster County. A microburst also occurred in York County, where widespread tree damage was observed near Brogue.
episodes.213982: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed across portions of northeastern Oklahoma during the late afternoon of the 13th, along a pre-existing outflow boundary from earlier organized thunderstorms that moved through Arkansas. The atmosphere became very unstable during the afternoon across the region, and deep layer wind shear was strong. This combination resulted in several supercell thunderstorms developing, which produced large hail up to two inches in diameter and damaging wind gusts. ||Thunderstorms also developed along a cold front stretching across south central Kansas during the late afternoon and early evening. These thunderstorms moved southeast across northeastern Oklahoma during the evening and organized into a squall line, which produced a number of damaging wind reports.

Thunderstorms repeatedly developed and moved over the same areas along the boundary, producing very heavy rainfall across portions of coastal Mississippi over the two-day period and resulting in flash flooding.

episodes.214658: A mid-level disturbance rotated through cyclonic northwest flow established over the Northern Plains. episodes.214693: A strong line of thunderstorms swept across West Virginia on the afternoon of June 14th ahead of a cold front. The environment that day was conducive for storms to thrive, and reached strengths that caused a swath of tree and power line damage from the Ohio River to the Appalachian Mountains. The line of storms continued to steadily shift eastward with the arrival of the cold front that evening, with the risk of damaging wind gusts also coming to an end.
episodes.214752: A stationary front extended along the I-20 corridor of East Texas and North Louisiana during the morning and afternoon hours of June 15th, with a warm, very moist, and unstable air mass present south of the front. In fact, the vertical extent of the deep layer moisture profile was the greatest on record for the calendar day, and provided the fuel needed as a weak upper level disturbance moving into the region from the west enhanced large scale forcing within this very moist air mass. As a result, clusters of showers and thunderstorms containing very heavy rainfall developed along and south of I-20, producing excessively heavy hourly rainfall amounts of 2-3+ inches per hour across portions of Lower East Texas and North Louisiana. Widespread rainfall amounts of 1-3 inches, with isolated higher amounts in excess of 5 inches were observed, falling over a brief period of time which resulted in flash flooding.
episodes.214754: A stationary front extended along the I-20 corridor of East Texas and North Louisiana during the morning and afternoon hours of June 15th, with a warm, very moist, and unstable air mass present south of the front. In fact, the vertical extent of the deep layer moisture profile was the greatest on record for the calendar day, and provided the fuel needed as a weak upper level disturbance moving into the region from the west enhanced large scale forcing within this very moist air mass. As a result, clusters of showers and thunderstorms containing very heavy rainfall developed along and south of I-20, producing excessively heavy hourly rainfall amounts of 2-3+ inches per hour across portions of Lower East Texas and North Louisiana. Widespread rainfall amounts of 1-3 inches, with isolated higher amounts in excess of 5 inches were observed, falling over a brief period of time which resulted in flash flooding. 5.11 inches of rain was measured in Marshall in Central Harrison County from these storms.
episodes.215090: A cold front moved into South-Central Texas and stalled. The airmass the front moved into was warm and very moist. Thunderstorms formed in the vicinity of the front and some of these storms produced locally heavy rain that led to flash flooding.
episodes.215138: A stalled frontal boundary over eastern North Carolina and southern Virginia interacted with an upper-level system to produce isolated severe storms across Sampson, Halifax, Nash, Guilford, and Johnston Counties.
episodes.215452: Aided by a cold front and a shortwave, a strong line of thunderstorms developed in central Ohio and quickly progressed east across western Pennsylvania and northern West Virginia. A moisture rich environment with mid to upper 60s dew points and mid 70s temperatures supported a favorable setup with MLCAPE values around 1000 J/kg and strong effective shear of 40-50 knots. Widespread swaths of wind damage were noted with 60-80 mph wind, and plenty of low level shear also supported embedded mesovortices and transient tornadoes within the line of thunderstorms.
episodes.215473: Thunderstorms brought isolated flash flooding to the Heartland.
episodes.215640: Scattered storms developed across portions of central and eastern Virginia on June 14. These storms produced damaging winds and isolated large hail.
episodes.215641: Scattered storms developed across portions of central and eastern Virginia on June 14 before crossing the Chesapeake Bay and moving into the Lower Maryland Eastern Shore. Isolated damaging wind gusts continued as the storms moved across Maryland.
episodes.215642: Scattered storms developed across portions of central and eastern Virginia on June 14. These storms produced gusty winds as they moved over portions of the Chesapeake Bay, Lower James River, and York River.
episodes.215670: A weak frontal boundary drifted into southeast Texas well ahead of Tropical Storm Arthur. Heavy rain produced areas of flooding.
episodes.215671: A strong thunderstorm developed as a frontal boundary moved through Luzerne County in Northeast Pennsylvania. Stronger gusts associated with this storm resulted in a couple of downed trees.
episodes.215703: Tropical Storm Arthur made landfall along the coast of southeast Texas and moved northeast across central Louisiana. Heavy rain trained across portions of central Louisiana creating widespread flooding and a new rainfall record. Flood waters slowly drained in the days following the passage of the system.
episodes.215712: The dryline pushed to about the Rio Grande Valley while a subtle upper level disturbance moved through southwest flow helping to produce severe thunderstorms and flash flooding.  Many locations across El Paso reported over 1 inch of rainfall with the thunderstorms.
episodes.215713: The dryline pushed west towards the Rio Grande Valley and a subtle upper level disturbance in southwest flow helped to trigger severe thunderstorms with strong winds and heavy rain. Almost 2 inches of rain was reported with some of these storms.
episodes.215741: A repeating band of slow-moving showers and thunderstorms over the Weslaco/Donna area during the early to mid morning of June 15th produced areas of notable flash flooding.  Up to 7 inches of rain fell in a little more than two hours, leaving some streets with up to three feet of water depth and water into several properties. Another round of thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon across Starr and Jim Hogg County, with urban flooding across portions of Rio Grande City based on an estimated 3-5 of rainfall there.

episodes.215786: Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed late in the day, producing a few strong to severe thunderstorms made it into New Jersey and produced damaging wind gusts.

On June 15, 2026, a survey team from the National Weather Service|Baltimore/Washington Weather Forecast Office conducted a formal|storm assessment in Frederick County, Maryland. The objective of|the field survey was to analyze the thunderstorm wind damage that|occurred during the evening of Sunday, June 14, 2026. The event|began at approximately 7:30 PM EDT, when a cluster of showers|initiated in central Jefferson County, West Virginia. This|convective system tracked continuously northeastward into|Frederick County, Maryland, while exhibiting steady|intensification.||As the storm progressed east of Libertytown, Maryland, it|generated a localized zone of significant structural and tree|damage. The most severe impacts were concentrated within the 9000|block of Bessie Clemson Road. Based on the degree of damage|observed, peak wind velocities in this specific corridor were|estimated up to 80 MPH. Physical evidence at the scene included|numerous snapped and uprooted soft and hardwood trees, alongside|the total wall collapse of a barn structure.||Analysis of the debris field and fallen vegetation revealed a|strictly unidirectional damage pattern. This uniform orientation|aligned precisely with the forward motion of the storm, confirming|the absence of rotational characteristics. Therefore, the|National Weather Service Baltimore/Washington Weather Forecast|Office has classified the destruction as a straight-line wind|event driven by downburst winds.||Outside of the immediate Bessie Clemson Road impact zone, the|thunderstorm produced sporadic wind damage across the broader|county. These widespread convective wind gusts were estimated to|range from 60 to 80 mph with all associated damage matching the|directional trajectory of the storm.

Torrential rainfall the began just before the morning commute would soon add up to notable flash flooding across Weslaco, parts of Mercedes, and extending westward to the east side of Donna and southward to near US 281 (Progreso). Rainfall totals of near 7 inches were recorded along IH-2 near the Mid-Valley Airport, in just over two hours. Flash flooding included numerous streets, including the frontage road, with 2-3 feet of water as well as several properties with water incursion into them. Some of the reports included:|*Numerous social media reports and news media coverage of flooding along the I-2 frontage road in Weslaco near North Republic St and North Texas Blvd.|*The IH-2 frontage road was closed (eastbound) between Westgate and Texas Boulevard (Exits 157 to 155).  |*A city disaster declaration was issued by the Mayor of Weslaco due to the extensive nature of the flooding.
